newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN FISH FIRMS SEE HOPE IN LOBSTER DIE-OFF.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN FISH FIRMS SEE HOPE IN LOBSTER DIE-OFF.

text.p: Some members of South Africa's fishing industry believe a massive lobster die-off on the Atlantic coast in recent weeks is a sign the resource is richer than was thought, an industry spokesman said on Thursday.
But a government fisheries scientist, Andy Cockroft, dismissed the idea as wishful thinking.

An estimated 800 to 1,500 tonnes of lobster have died in the Elands Bay area 200 km (125 miles) along the coast north of Cape Town in the last three weeks because of algae blooms that deplete oxygen in the water.

The figure compares with a total allowable catch (TAC) quota for the area of 400 tonnes set by the government to prevent over-fishing. The national TAC this year is 1,700 tonnes, much of it exported to Japan.
The industry spokesman, who asked not to be identified, said it was too early to assess what the impact of the die-off would be on commercial producers but added:

"Something that has surprised many people is the amount of fish that came ashore in a very small area. Some people are saying 'if that's the amount, the state of the resource has been underestimated considerably'."
The spokesman said that in contrast to fears that the lobster resource was under pressure, the die-off could show that "there's a lot more fish out there than anyone thought".
But Cockroft said the number of lobsters that had died, most of them undersized, was consistent with government estimates of the size of the resource.
"The industry would like to think there were more than anyone thought, but if you look at the figures, that wasn't the case at all," he said.
"The die-off was startling, an in-your-face kind of picture, but we're not surprised that that amount came out."
He said the lobster resource in the area would take four or five years to recover. Catch quotas are set at about 30 percent of the estimated total adult lobster bio-mass.
